title: Amos 9:11–15
context: The book closes with a promise. In that day the LORD will raise up the fallen tent of David, repair its breaches, and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations called by the LORD’s name. The land will be so fruitful that the plowman overtakes the reaper; the LORD will bring his people back from captivity, they will rebuild and plant, and they will never again be plucked up from their land. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise in light of the covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7. In Acts 15:16–18 James cites this passage at the Jerusalem council, in wording that differs from Amos at points; the two passages can be read side by side without merging them. Readers in both traditions hold several options for the land and planting promises: restoration after the exile, fulfillment in Christ and the church, or a future restoration of Israel. These notes present them as options, with no winner between the traditions.

verses.text: In that day I will raise up the tent of David who is fallen and close up its breaches, and I will raise up its ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old,
verses.arminianNotes: In that day I will raise up the tent of David who is fallen and close up its breaches, Arminian readers see the restoration of David’s house after judgment, read in light of 2 Samuel 7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Davidic promise as shared ground (2 Samuel 7:16), compare Hosea 3:5. Acts 15:16 cites this verse at the Jerusalem council, using the words “the tabernacle of David”.

verses.text: that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name,” says the LORD who does this.
verses.arminianNotes: that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name, Arminian readers often see here the gospel reaching the nations, as James applies it in Acts 15:17.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Acts 15:17 reads “that the rest of men may seek after the Lord”, wording that differs from “possess the remnant of Edom”. Readers in both traditions take the verse as Israel’s rule over neighbors or as the nations gathered to the LORD.

verses.text: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills.
verses.arminianNotes: that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, Arminian readers see abundance so great that the seasons run together, harvest following harvest and sowing following vintage without pause.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of sweet wine dripping from the mountains, similar to Joel 3:18. Some read it as restored land, others as a picture of blessing in Christ’s kingdom.

verses.text: I will bring my people Israel back from captivity, and they will rebuild the ruined cities, and inhabit them; and they will plant vineyards, and drink wine from them. They shall also make gardens, and eat their fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: I will bring my people Israel back from captivity, Arminian readers see restoration from exile, with cities rebuilt and vineyards planted, a reversal of the curses of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the promise is read by some as return from exile, by others as fulfilled in the church, and by others as future restoration of Israel, held across both traditions.

verses.text: I will plant them on their land, and they will no more be plucked up out of their land which I have given them,” says the LORD your God.
verses.arminianNotes: I will plant them on their land, Arminian readers see a promise of security: they will no more be plucked up out of their land, closing the book with hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Jeremiah 31:28, where the LORD watches over his people to build and to plant. Shared ground: the LORD your God secures the final word of restoration.
